title: “How bad is it?” “We're broke.” The budget crunch the next president actually inherits
dek: In the 2000 episode, President Lisa Simpson's first question is about the money Trump left behind. The real answer in 2026: a $1.99 trillion deficit, more than $1 trillion a year in interest, a gross debt past $40 trillion. What is on the desk on Jan. 20, 2029, and how much of it carries this administration's name.
body:
In the Oval Office of “Bart to the Future,” President Lisa Simpson's first question to her cabinet is about money. “As you know, we've inherited quite a budget crunch from President Trump,” she says. “How bad is it?” Secretary Milhouse Van Houten holds up a chart and answers: “We're broke” [8][9]. The episode aired in March 2000, when the federal government was running a surplus. Whoever takes the oath on Jan. 20, 2029 will not need Milhouse's chart. The Treasury's own statement for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30 shows a deficit of $1.99 trillion, interest costs above $1 trillion for the first time, and a gross national debt that passed $40 trillion in August [1][2][3]. This report lays out what the 48th president actually inherits, whoever she or he turns out to be, and how much of it has the current administration's name on it.

## How bad is it

The fiscal 2026 deficit came in at $1.992 trillion, $217 billion more than the $1.775 trillion of fiscal 2025, a 12 percent increase in a single year [1][2]. Receipts were a record $5.40 trillion, up 3 percent; outlays were a record $7.40 trillion, up 6 percent [1]. Measured against the economy, the Treasury estimated the gap at 6.2 percent of GDP, up from 5.8 percent the year before [1].

Reuters called it the largest shortfall since the pandemic year of fiscal 2021, when the deficit reached $2.77 trillion, and the third-largest in history [1]. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a deficit-hawk group, put it another way: the largest deficit the country has ever run outside a war or a recession [3]. Its president, Maya MacGuineas, said debt held by the public is now about as large as the entire economy's annual output [3].

The month that closed the year tells the same story in miniature. September 2026 showed a $27 billion deficit; September 2025 had shown a $198 billion surplus [1]. The difference is partly timing, but the direction is not in dispute. The Congressional Budget Office's own tally of the year, published a week before the Treasury's, matched it: a $2.0 trillion deficit, $218 billion wider than the year before, with receipts up $169 billion and outlays up $386 billion [6].

## We're broke, measured

Milhouse's two words are not literally true. The United States borrows in its own currency and has never missed a payment. But the stock of what it owes has crossed a line that no president has inherited before.

The gross national debt passed $40 trillion in August [1][2]. The Treasury's Debt to the Penny count on Oct. 14 read $40,329,229,827,541.02 [2]. The more meaningful measure, debt held by the public, which strips out what the government owes its own trust funds, stood at about 99 percent of GDP at the end of 2025 and reaches 101 percent in 2026 on CBO's February projection [7][5]. The record is 106 percent, set in 1946 at the end of the Second World War; on CBO's path the debt passes it in 2030, the next president's second year in office, and reaches 120 percent of GDP by 2036 [7][5].

For scale, the Simpsons' advisers told Lisa the country had “borrowed from every country in the world” [8]. The real version is less colorful and more expensive, because the borrowing has a running cost.

## The interest bill

This is the part of the inheritance that was not there in 2000, or in 2016, or in 2021. Net interest on the federal debt was $352 billion in 2021 [7]. In fiscal 2026 it passed $1 trillion for the first time, about $1.1 trillion, or a record 3.4 percent of GDP [2][7]. The Treasury's broader debt-service line, which counts interest paid to the trust funds as well, hit a record $1.36 trillion, up 12 percent in a year [1]. On that measure, interest now trails only Social Security and the combined health programs; on the narrower net-interest measure, it costs more than Medicare and more than defense, and less than Social Security [1][2][3].

CBO's director, Phillip Swagel, told Fortune in late October that growth alone will not fix this. “It's a structural deficit, it's large, we have to address it,” he said [4]. The agency's projection has interest at $1.2 trillion this year and a little under $2.5 trillion a year by 2036, roughly $200 billion a month and about double what the country is projected to spend on defense that year [4]. Added up, the ten years from 2026 to 2036 cost $20.1 trillion in interest alone [4]. The Peterson Foundation's reading of the same CBO numbers puts the ten-year interest total at $16.2 trillion and the 2036 figure at $2.1 trillion; the difference is in what is counted and when the projection was made, and either number is larger than the whole federal budget was in the year the episode aired [7].

## What the Trump years added, and what they took away

A president's inheritance is never entirely the predecessor's doing. Deficits near 6 percent of GDP predate this administration, since fiscal 2025 ran at 5.8 percent, and the trust-fund arithmetic [1] that drives most of the growth was set decades ago. But CBO has put numbers on the two biggest choices of the past two years.

The 2025 reconciliation law, Public Law 119-21, which the White House calls the One Big Beautiful Bill, added an estimated $4.7 trillion to projected deficits over the decade, counting its effects on the economy and on debt service [5]. Higher tariffs, as of February, were projected to take $3.0 trillion off them over the same period [5]. That was before the Supreme Court. In February the court struck down the administration's blanket tariffs, and the government began refunding importers; by the end of the fiscal year the refunds totaled $144.6 billion, nearly halving gross customs receipts of $317.8 billion [2]. Net tariff income for the year fell 11 percent, to about $173 billion, and the refunds alone pushed the deficit roughly $140 billion above CBO's February forecast [1][2]. A third phase of refunds is under way, so the number is not final [2].

The revenue side softened in another way. Corporate income tax collections fell about 16 percent in 2026, as the new law's larger deductions offset the growth in corporate profits [2]. On the spending side, a Bloomberg Government analysis cited by Yahoo Finance singled out the Department of Homeland Security, whose budget rose 146 percent from 2025 to 2026 [2]. Interest, benefit programs, defense and education accounted for most of the rest of the $386 billion increase in outlays [6]. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has focused on the tariff refunds, which have turned tariffs into a cost to the government in recent months, and administration officials have described the year's figure as a blip [2].

## What is on the desk on Jan. 20, 2029

Take CBO's February path as the baseline, and adjust for a year that came in about $140 billion worse than planned [2]. The next president inherits:

- **A deficit of about $2 trillion a year, and rising.** CBO's projection has deficits of $1.9 trillion in 2026 and 2027 and $3.1 trillion by 2036, when they would equal 6.7 percent of GDP [5][7]. Swagel's agency describes the gap as structural, around 6 percent of GDP whatever the economy does [4].
- **An interest bill larger than the defense budget**, already true in 2026 and widening every year of the projection [3][4].
- **Debt held by the public at its all-time record** sometime in 2030, the second year of the term, on the current path [7][5].
- **Two trust funds running dry on the watch.** Fortune reported in October that Social Security's fund is a little over seven years from running out and Medicare's about six and a half, which puts Medicare's inside the 2029–2033 term and Social Security's right around its end [4].
- **A target that would require halving the deficit.** CRFB's proposal is a deficit of 3 percent of GDP, which MacGuineas described as half the current level [3].

The Simpsons' version of this meeting ended with an adviser proposing cyanide pills and Bart charming the creditors into waiting [8]. The real one will end with Treasury auctions, which have not failed, and a budget resolution, which usually does.

## A note on the joke

The line works in 2029 whoever is sitting in the chair, which is part of why it has lasted. It would be true for a President Ossoff or a President Vance as surely as for a President Ocasio-Cortez, and it was true, in a smaller way, for President Biden in 2021, when a Media Matters editor tweeted it beside a CNN column about Trump leaving “a mess” and Snopes had to point out that the column was about cyberattacks [9]. The budget crunch is bipartisan in origin and nonpartisan in arrival.

What has changed since 2000 is the unit of measurement. Lisa's writers imagined a country that was broke in the way a family is broke: creditors at the door. The country that the next president inherits is not that. It is a country paying $1.1 trillion a year to keep the door open, with the bill rising faster than anything else in the budget [2][4]. Milhouse's chart, redrawn with the real numbers, is on The Watch's [Prophecy Watch](https://bboldt86.github.io/lanscape-navigator/news/prophecy/) page. The answer to “How bad is it?” has a decimal point now.
